title: Forklift Mast Drive Shaft: Sub-Assembly Design
short_description: Full stress-driven design of a power-transmission shaft for a forklift lift mechanism — load analysis, chain drive, bearings and manufacturing route.
full_description: An individual mechanical design coursework project taking a chain-driven forklift lift shaft from a hand-sketched layout through to a fully justified engineering design: reaction forces, bending/torque diagrams, chain drive selection, iterative shaft sizing, bearing selection, materials selection and a manufacturing cost analysis.
motivation: The brief was to design a complete shaft sub-assembly for a chain-driven forklift lift mechanism: a horizontal shaft on two bearings, carrying a central driven sprocket fed by a motor chain and two outboard sprockets driving the mast lift chains — with every dimension and component choice mechanically justified rather than assumed.
methodology: Starting from a dimensioned shaft layout sketch, free-body diagrams in both planes were solved for reactions, then shear-force, bending-moment and torque diagrams were built via Macaulay's method. Chain drive was selected using a service-factor method against BS chain rating tables, giving a 31.75mm-pitch triplex chain. Shaft geometry was sized iteratively across four passes, computing combined bending/torsion stress with stress-concentration factors at each node against the material's allowable stress. Bearings were selected via SKF methodology, checking equivalent dynamic load against L10 life. Materials were shortlisted using an Ashby merit-index chart (M = √E/ρ), and the turning operation was analysed for material removal rate, machining time, cutting force and cost. Circlips (to DIN 471) and a keyway (to BS 4235-1) were sized by shear and bearing stress checks.
results: The design converged on a 60mm bearing diameter with an SKF 212-2Z deep-groove ball bearing (C = 56.1kN), giving an L10 life of roughly 357 million revolutions. An aluminium/silicon-carbide metal-matrix composite was selected as the shaft material. The turning operation was shown viable on a 10kW lathe at a machining cost of approximately £11.35, with a 114mm shaft diameter, a 36×20mm key sized at 107mm length, and DIN 471 circlips at each of the four groove locations.
